study.title: Digital Blueprint
study.question: How do I plan a digital product before building it?
study.passage:
Planning guide (written for this lesson):
1. Choose a format that fits your problem statement and skills: an app or game (Scratch, MIT App Inventor, Code.org), a website (Google Sites or simple HTML), or a video (phone camera and free editing software).
2. List features. Sort them into "must have" (the MVP) and "nice to have." For a homework reminder: must have = add a task with a due date, see tasks in date order, show a reminder; nice to have = colours by subject, sound effects.
3. Storyboard or wireframe: For an app or website, draw each screen as a wireframe with buttons labelled and arrows showing what each button does. For a video, storyboard each shot with a sketch, the shot type, what is said and the length.
4. Task list: Break the build into tasks of 20 minutes or less and order them.

body.hook: A computer does exactly what you tell it, nothing more and nothing less. "Make a sandwich" means nothing to a robot; "pick up bread, open the jar, spread 1 tbsp peanut butter" does. Coding is giving clear, ordered instructions.

A named storage space for a value that can change, such as a score.

study.title: Build the Logic
study.question: How do sequence, loops and conditionals make a digital product work?
study.passage:
Coding concepts (written for this lesson, shown in plain steps that match Scratch or App Inventor blocks):
Sequence: when the app starts → show the title → show the task list.
Loop: for each task in the list → show its name and due date.
Conditional: if the due date is tomorrow → show the task in red and play a reminder; else → show it in black.
Variable: set "tasks due" to 0; for each task due this week, change "tasks due" by 1; show "You have [tasks due] tasks this week."
Unplugged warm-up: In pairs, one person writes an algorithm to draw a house on grid paper using only "move up/down/left/right [number]" and "pen up/pen down." The partner follows it exactly. Did the house come out right?
Build task: Build the MVP screen from your wireframe using at least one loop, one conditional and one variable. For a video project, use the same logic to plan an edit sequence: if a shot is longer than 6 seconds → trim it.

body.objective: Students will be able to debug and refine.
successCriteria: I can find bugs using a step-by-step strategy
I can fix bugs and explain what caused them
I can refine my product so it works reliably
body.hook: The word "bug" became famous in computing when, in 1947, engineers found a real moth stuck in a computer relay and taped it into the logbook. Today every programmer spends a lot of time finding and fixing bugs. Debugging is a skill, not bad luck.

vocabulary.definition: A mistake in code or a product that makes it work incorrectly.
A message the software shows when something goes wrong.
To follow code step by step to see what it does.
An unusual input that might break a product, such as an empty list.
To make small improvements so a product works better.

study.title: Bug Hunt
study.question: How do I find and fix problems in my digital product?
study.passage:
Debugging strategy (written for this lesson):
1. Reproduce: Make the bug happen again on purpose. Write down exactly what you did.
2. Isolate: Find the smallest part of the code where it goes wrong. Turn blocks off or add a "say" block to show a variable's value.
3. Trace: Follow the code step by step. What did you expect? What actually happened?
4. Fix one thing: Change one thing, then test again.
5. Check edge cases: empty list, a date in the past, a very long task name, pressing a button twice.
Sample bugs to fix:
Bug A: The task counter shows 0 even when there are tasks. (The counter is reset to 0 inside the loop instead of before it.)
Bug B: Every task shows in red. (The condition checks "due date ≥ tomorrow" instead of "due date = tomorrow.")
Bug C: The app crashes when the list is empty. (The code reads item 1 without checking the list has items.)
For videos: check audio levels, spelling in titles, jump cuts and length.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; the 1947 moth story is from the Harvard Mark II logbook.
